PULITZER PRIZE WINNER • An epic, extraordinary account of scientific rivalry and obsession in the quest to survey all of life on Earth

WINNER OF THE PEN/E.O. WILSON LITERARY SCIENCE WRITING AWARD • A KIRKUS REVIEWS BEST BOOK OF THE YEAR
In the eighteenth century, two men—exact contemporaries and polar opposites—dedicated their lives to the same daunting task: identifying and describing all life on Earth. Carl Linnaeus, a pious Swedish doctor with a huckster’s flair, believed that life belonged in tidy, static categories. Georges-Louis de Buffon, an aristocratic polymath and keeper of France’s royal garden, viewed life as a dynamic swirl of complexities. Each began his task believing it to be difficult but not impossible: How could the planet possibly hold more than a few thousand species—or as many could fit on Noah’s Ark?
Both fell far short of their goal, but in the process they articulated starkly divergent views on nature, the future of the Earth, and humanity itself. Linnaeus gave the world such concepts as mammal, primate, and Homo sapiens, but he also denied that species change and he promulgated racist pseudoscience. Buffon formulated early prototypes of evolution and genetics, warned of global climate change, and argued passionately against prejudice. The clash of their conflicting worldviews continued well after their deaths, as their successors contended for dominance in the emerging science that came to be called biology.
In Every Living Thing, Jason Roberts weaves a sweeping, unforgettable narrative spell, exploring the intertwined lives and legacies of Linnaeus and Buffon—as well as the groundbreaking, often fatal adventures of their acolytes—to trace an arc of insight and discovery that extends across three centuries into the present day.

# EVERY LIVING THING

### THE GREAT AND DEADLY RACE TO KNOW ALL LIFE

by Jason Roberts ‧ RELEASE DATE: April 9, 2024

A lively, panoramic contribution to the history of science.

Exciting chronicle of the battle “to complete a comprehensive accounting of all life on Earth.”

Roberts, author of A Sense of the World, traces the lives and careers of two 18th-century naturalists whose opposing perspectives made them, and their followers, rivals: Carl Linnaeus, a misogynist self-promoter and holder of a “diploma-mill medical degree,” invented binary nomenclature and a classification system that assigned plants and animals into kingdoms, classes, orders, families, and species. George-Louis de Buffon, an aristocratic natural historian in charge of France’s royal gardens, saw the natural world as thrillingly complex. Linnaeus believed that life on Earth was unchanged from the moment of God’s creation. “It was against faith,” Roberts writes, “to envision new species coming into existence, or existing ones fading into extinction.” De Buffon, on the other hand, believed all such systematic approaches were reductionist and flawed, and that of Linnaeus, “the least sensible and the most monstrous.” Species, he posited, changed by adapting to their environments. Both men defended their views in widely read tracts: De Buffon’s 35-volume Histoire Naturelle, Générale et Particuliere reflected his own minute investigations; Linnaeus, author of continual revisions to his Systema Naturae, sent acolytes to conduct research in the field, where they sometimes perished. Because of his “easily grasped classification system,” which included racist classifications of humans, Linnaeus prevailed, while de Buffon’s reputation plummeted. Roberts examines the men’s legacies as natural philosophy became science, and science branched into biology, zoology, and genetics. Linnaeus’ systems were complicated by the discovery of microscopic life and blooming biodiversity; towering figures confronted the stark evidence of evolution. Among the scientists that feature in this well-populated narrative are George Cuvier, Darwin, Thomas Henry Huxley, Agassiz, Mendel, and Hugo de Vries, each confronting the controversy incited by Linnaeus and de Buffon.

A lively, panoramic contribution to the history of science.

L38@P1: Patrick J. Boyer has succeeded marvellously in bringing to light a remarkable
L39@P1: tale from Ontario’s pioneering days, namely Thomas Osborne’s Reluctant Pioneer:
L40@P1: How I Survived Five Years in the Canadian
L41@P1: Bush. The autobiographical account traces
L42@P1: the adventures of an individual whose
L43@P1: metamorphosis from boy to man occurred
L44@P1: in this region in the latter part of the nineteenth century. In the process of recounting this story, Reluctant Pioneer presents
L45@P1: an intriguing and compelling memoir, one
L46@P1: that adeptly demonstrates how such a simple life, which was practically defined by
L47@P1: adversity, could prove so deeply satisfying
L48@P1: and rewarding.
L49@P1: The story Reluctant Pioneer tells is an
L50@P1: extraordinarily interesting one. On the
L51@P1: cusp of his sixteenth birthday in 1875,
L52@P1: Thomas Osborne is summarily summoned
L53@P1: to Muskoka from Philadelphia by his father; the latter had moved his family from
L54@P1: England to the United States roughly one
L55@P1: decade earlier in the hope of improving its
L56@P1: lot. Although nearly the entire Osborne
L57@P1: clan initially moved to Muskoka, only Thomas, his father, and his younger brother
L58@P1: remain for the long term after it becomes
L59@P1: abundantly clear that the hardscrabble,
L60@P1: pioneering existence was suitable for only
L61@P1: the hardiest members of their family.
L62@P1: The bulk of the book is thus devoted to
L63@P1: Thomas Osborne providing a lively and entertaining account of the trials and tribulations that confronted him, his brother and
L64@P1: their father in Muskoka during the mid- to
L65@P1: late 1870s. Osborne’s graphic description
L66@P1: of this period reminds us that it is a time, as
L67@P1: Roy MacGregor aptly puts it in the book’s
L68@P1: Foreword, “so far in our past that we have
L69@P1: largely lost the ability to imagine it”. For
L70@P1: example, every facet of the Osbornes’ lives
L71@P1: in Muskoka involved the expenditure of
L72@P1: energy in volumes that seem unimaginable
L73@P1: today. Travelling to town entailed either
L74@P1: walking (often through dense bush), or
L75@P1: rowing or paddling one of their boats (often through choppy waters), for the better
L76@P1: part of two days. Similarly, the mere act of
L77@P1: eating was a near-constant enterprise that
L78@P1: consisted of killing, growing, picking or
L79@P1: catching practically any form of nourishment that would help fend off starvation;
L80@P1: Osborne resorted at one of his lowest points
L81@P1-2: to reviving his withering body by consum272 ONTARIO HISTORY
L82@P2: ing dried grass that protruded through the
L83@P2: snow. Such an austere existence caused the
L84@P2: Osbornes to rejoice at their good fortune
L85@P2: in being able to consume “treats” such as
L86@P2: porcupine soup, “edible jelly” from a fish
L87@P2: head, or beaver tails (not the deep-fried
L88@P2: and sugar-dusted variety!), but even they
L89@P2: had to admit that downing crow and loon
L90@P2: was a non-starter because these birds were
L91@P2: too tough to stomach! Likewise, staying
L92@P2: warm and guarding against the swarms of
L93@P2: bugs compelled them to be perpetually
L94@P2: felling trees and then bucking and splitting
L95@P2: the logs, and applying a repulsive bug dope
L96@P2: elixir that consisted of pork fat and black
L97@P2: tar. Boyer smartly adds an Afterword that
L98@P2: provides the reader with a thumbnail history of what ultimately became of the Osbornes, an ending to the story that will not
L99@P2: be spoiled here.
L100@P2: While the tale Reluctant Pioneer tells
L101@P2: makes the book well worth reading, its
L102@P2: boasts numerous other strengths. In terms
L103@P2: of style, its prose is simple and accessible,
L104@P2: and paints a wonderfully complete and
L105@P2: vivid picture of both the range and depth
L106@P2: of the Osbornes’ pioneering struggles. The
L107@P2: writing is also sprinkled with wry observations that periodically inject measured doses of humour into the story. The “first few
L108@P2: days in Muskoka”, the author dryly notes,
L109@P2: “we had a great time, what with the flies, oil
L110@P2: of tar, pork fat, and the smoke from the fire
L111@P2: in the cabin”. In addition, Osborne tells his
L112@P2: story with a healthy cadence that provides
L113@P2: sufficient detail without overwhelming the
L114@P2: reader with it.
L115@P2: The book’s content is truly its most
L116@P2: powerful asset, and for several reasons. As
L117@P2: far as Canadian literature in general and
L118@P2: history in particular are concerned, Osborne’s tale represents an all too rare foil
L119@P2: to the prevailing dour and loathsome perspective on the homesteading existence.
L120@P2: Whereas a host of authors have portrayed
L121@P2: this experience as having been mired in a
L122@P2: sea of dreadful despair, Osborne conversely depicts it as having been one drenched
L123@P2: in delightful difficulty. Although his life
L124@P2: in Muskoka was a practically continuous
L125@P2: struggle against substantial challenges, Osborne remained decidedly sanguine about
L126@P2: life and deeply in love with it. He did not
L127@P2: actively seek thrills, and yet he revelled in
L128@P2: enduring the terrifying moments that came
L129@P2: his way on what seemed like a daily basis.
L130@P2: And it is through relaying these stories
L131@P2: that the book delivers a truly profound
L132@P2: message. As much as Osborne’s life is filled
L133@P2: with hardship, persevering through those
L134@P2: incessantly trying experiences imbues his
L135@P2: life with a meaning that is so sweet and
L136@P2: rich. Frantically paddling through storms
L137@P2: on a lake or surviving encounters with
L138@P2: bears are all incidents that drive home how
L139@P2: the difficulties that complicated Osborne’s
L140@P2: life were also the factors that made it all
L141@P2: the more worth living. Merely to survive
L142@P2: until nightfall was the ultimate aim when
L143@P2: he arose each day, and as mundane as his
L144@P2: routine may have been, it exemplified an
L145@P2: approach that fully embraced life by exalting its simplest pleasures and against which
L146@P2: our own world of instant gratification
L147@P2: seems sadly superficial in comparison.
L148@P2: Similarly, the book offers much food
L149@P2: for thought for the environmental historian. On the one hand, Reluctant Pioneer
L150@P2: highlights how distant we have grown
L151@P2: from recognizing our dependence on nature. Whereas today we are rarely exercised about the source of our next meal,
L152@P2: Osborne’s life revolved around such basic
L153@P2: concerns. On the other hand, his approach
L154@P2: to acquiring his daily sustenance reminds us
L155@P2: of the degree to which we have constructed
L156@P2: an artificial world of socially permissible
L157@P2: behaviours towards our flora and fauna.
L158@P2: He does not think twice about shooting
L159@P2-3: salmon and trout that congregate near the book reviews 273
L160@P3: shore of a local lake or spearing them by
L161@P3: jacklight. Likewise, he nets as many fish as
L162@P3: he can and hunts to kill as much game as he
L163@P3: is able without regard to conservation regulations; on one occasion he brazenly dismisses a game warden’s admonition about
L164@P3: fishing out of season with the retort, “there
L165@P3: is no law here”. Finally, he jubilantly screams
L166@P3: “Hurrah” after having killed a bear that
L167@P3: had been ravaging his family’s corn crops.
L168@P3: To Osborne these were simply questions
L169@P3: of survival, whereas today such behaviour
L170@P3: would be likely to draw gasps and scorn.
L171@P3: Ultimately, this book amply rewards
L172@P3: its readers with an elegant ode to a simpler
L173@P3: way of life and the unadulterated joys it delivered. As a result, Boyer’s peroration is an
L174@P3: apposite one. “What we celebrate in Reluctant Pioneer”, he writes on the book’s final
L175@P3: page, “is not only the resilient adaptability
L176@P3: of humans, nor even the act of survival itself, but above all else the spirit of optimistic realism which infuses both”.
L177@P3: Mark Kuhlberg

# Mystery around top-ranked Rockefeller book grows as university publisher denies involvement

January 28, 2025 by admin 0 Comments

Image

Wealth

A print copy of “The 38 Letters from J.D. Rockefeller to his son: Perspective, Ideology and Wisdom” purchased on Amazon.

CNBC

The mystery around a top-selling Amazon book attributed to John D. Rockefeller has grown to include a university publisher, which denies any involvement in the book despite being listed as it’s publisher.

CNBC began raising questions last month about the authenticity of “The 38 Letters from J.D. Rockefeller to his son: Perspective, Ideology and Wisdom,” a purported collection of letters by John D. Rockefeller Sr. sold on Amazon, Barnes & Noble and other sites.

The mysterious origin of “The 38 Letters” raises a host of questions about publishing and the surge in wealth-help books.

The book is ranked No. 22 on Amazon’s list of best-selling economic history books, yet it’s filled with factual errors and the letters often bear little resemblance to Rockefeller’s other writings, CNBC previously reported.

The Rockefeller Archive Center, whose mission includes preserving and cataloguing Rockefeller family history for philanthropy, said it was unable to find any letters from John D. Rockefeller Sr. or to John D. Rockefeller Jr. that match those in the book. It also cited major factual errors in book, including an incorrect year for John D. Rockefeller Jr.’s graduation from Brown as well as a supposed 1902 letter that mentioned Citibank, which wasn’t created until 1976.

“The authenticity of the book ‘The 38 Letters from J.D. Rockefeller to his Son’ is questionable,” the Archive center told CNBC in a statement.

Now caught in the confusion is OpenStax, the nonprofit publisher of open educational resources at Rice University, which is listed as the book’s publisher in some printings.

“We are not the publisher of this title,” a spokesperson for OpenStax told CNBC in a statement, adding that the publisher is “investigating the situation to protect our brand and ensure accurate information.”

## Get Inside Wealth directly to your inbox

Basic questions about the book remain unanswered: Who is the actual writer? How did it go unchallenged by so many readers for so long? Who’s profiting?

It’s popularity also highlights the enduring fascination with John D. Rockefeller, America’s first billionaire, and the vaunted Rockefeller family. Now in its seventh generation, with its wealth outshined by newer fortunes, the Rockefeller family name still holds almost mythical status around the world. Rockefeller-owned properties, artworks and personal items fetch hefty premiums when they come up for sale, from buyers around the world.

Works of art and personal items owned by Peggy and David Rockefeller, John D.’s grandson, fetched over $835 million at auction at Christie’s in 2018.

The Rockefeller name has even spawned a cottage industry in China of Rockefeller lessons and business advice.

“The 38 Letters” book has quickly became a popular financial- and parenting-advice book on Amazon, with 832 reviews on the book-selling site and an average review of 4.7 stars out of 5 on Amazon-owned review site Goodreads.
Barnes & Noble didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

John D. Rockefeller Sr.’s letters have been the subject of several authentic books. A book of letters edited by Archive Center Director Emeritus Joseph W. Ernst in 1994, titled “Dear Father, Dear Son: Correspondence of John D. Rockefeller and John D. Rockefeller Jr.” has 27 reviews on Amazon and a 4.1 average rating on Goodreads. Rockefeller Sr. also wrote “Random Reminiscences of Men and Events: In his own words, advice and perspective from the wealthiest man in history,” published in 1909.

The “38 Letters,” however, is filled with modern vernacular and unusual references. In some of the letters, John D. Sr., who was a devout Baptist, boasts about how he bested business rivals, made winning his chief mission in life and believed that being called “greedy” was high praise. “In my heart, I really reserved a place for greed,” one letter reads. “Greed is necessary!”

One letter states: “The first and last chapter of the Book of Wisdom states that ‘there is no free lunch in the world.'”

Intussen staat het boek wel in de lijst met bestsellers bij Barnes & Noble en Amazon. Het boek dat verkrijgbaar is in Nederland onder de ISBN codes  9788199968523  en  9781088177839 , staat ook op de website van Libris.
Het Rockefeller Archief Centrum laat desgevraagd weten dat zij niet in staat waren om brieven te vinden van J.D. Rockefeller, of aan zijn zoon Rockefeller Jr., die gelijkenis vertonen met de 38 brieven in het gepubliceerde en goed verkochte boek.

Het Rockefeller Archief Centrum trekt de authenticiteit van het boek dan ook in twijfel in hun reactie aan CNBC. OpenStax, een non-profit Rice University uitgever van educatieve documenten die in het boek vermeld wordt als de uitgever, ontkent in alle toonaarden: “Wij zijn niet de uitgever van deze titel”. # About the Guest

Image

Jennifer Garvey Berger

Jennifer Garvey Berger is endlessly curious about how humans grow — especially when things get messy, uncertain, and dizzyingly complex. A Harvard-trained researcher turned global leadership thinker, she has spent decades helping leaders untangle big questions and find more spacious, courageous, and effective ways to be in the world. As CEO and co-founder of Cultivating Leadership, she works with individuals and organizations to bring more wisdom, compassion, and genuine transformation into how people lead. All four of her books — Changing on the Job, Simple Habits for Complex Times, Unlocking Leadership Mindtraps, and Unleash Your Complexity Genius — are published by Stanford University Press. She is American by birth and now lives in the French countryside, where she bought a house with fourteen friends who are trying to keep the dogs from terrifying the cats — and to figure out, in quotidian terms, what it means to live and love well.

# Jennifer Garvey Berger

## Co-founder and CEO of Cultivating Leadership, coach, teacher, author

ImageJennifer Garvey Berger, Cultivating Leadership. 10th July 2018, London.

Jennifer believes that leadership is one of the most vital renewable resources in the world. In this topsy-turvy time, when uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity are raging, we need a new form of leadership for a new era. To that end, Jennifer designs and teaches leadership programs, coaches senior leaders and their teams, and supports new ways of thinking about strategy and people.

In her four highly acclaimed books, Unleash Your Complexity Genius (co-authored with Carolyn Coughlin), Unlocking Leadership Mindtraps, Simple Habits for Complex Times (co-authored with Keith Johnston), and Changing on the Job, Jennifer builds on deep theoretical knowledge to offer practical ways to make leaders’ organizations more successful, their work more meaningful, and their lives more gratifying.

Jennifer has worked with senior leaders in the private, non-profit, and government sectors around the world (like Novartis, Google, KPMG, Intel, Microsoft, Wikimedia, and the New Zealand Department of Conservation).

Jennifer is a co-founder and CEO of Cultivating leadership. She has a masters and a doctorate from Harvard University. Formerly an associate professor at George Mason University, Jennifer learned about deep change more than a decade ago when she turned down the tenure offer and moved to a small seaside village in New Zealand with her husband, two kids, and the family dog. While she still considers herself a Kiwi by choice, you can find her in the French countryside, where she has bought a house with eleven friends who live in community and try to keep the dog from terrifying the cats.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

L29: Information theory and inference, often taught separately, are here united in one entertaining textbook. These topics lie at the heart of many exciting areas of contemporary science and engineering - communication, signal processing, data mining, machine learning, pattern recognition, computational neuroscience, bioinformatics, and cryptography. This textbook introduces theory in tandem with applications.
L30: Information theory is taught alongside practical communication systems, such as arithmetic coding for data compression and sparse-graph codes for error-correction. A toolbox of inference techniques, including message-passing algorithms, Monte Carlo methods, and variational approximations, are developed alongside applications of these tools to clustering, convolutional codes, independent component analysis, and neural networks.
L31: The final part of the book describes the state of the art in error-correcting codes, including low-density parity-check codes, turbo codes, and digital fountain codes -- the twenty-first century standards for satellite communications, disk drives, and data broadcast. Richly illustrated, filled with worked examples and over 400 exercises, some with detailed solutions, David MacKay's groundbreaking book is ideal for self-learning and for undergraduate or graduate courses.
L32: Interludes on crosswords, evolution, and sex provide entertainment along the way. In sum, this is a textbook on information, communication, and coding for a new generation of students, and an unparalleled entry point into these subjects for professionals in areas as diverse as computational biology, financial engineering, and machine learning.

# Seretse & Ruth

Image: Front CoverWilf MbangaMerlin Press Limited, 2005 - Botswana - 387 pages In 1966 the Republic of Botswana came into existence, and this is the tale of how one family played a central role in the country's development. This biography focuses on the Khama family, and in particular, Seretse Khama: a statesman, chief, husband, and father. Dwelling on the last two aspects of this important figure, this account demonstrates how, in the face of great difficulties and opposition, Sereste and Ruth--a black man and a white woman--were united in a fruitful marriage that showed the world how people from different traditions might live happily. In many respects, their personal story, so movingly recounted here, mirrors the beliefs of the country itself, for Botswana has always stressed the importance of social harmony. Sereste was an Oxford-educated African king. She was a white Englishwoman working as a clerk at Lloyd's of London. Now their 1948 marriage, which caused scandal in Apartheid-stricken South Africa and the British protectorate of Bechuanaland (later Botswana), is to be the subject of a new period drama starring Britain's David Oyelowo and Rosamund Pike. Oyelowo is in talks to play Seretse Khama, who in 1965 became independent Botswana's first president. He was also kgosi (king) of the Bamangwato people, having been crowned at the age of four in 1925. Pike is in line to star as Ruth Williams, who would go on to be the first lady of Botswana between 1966 and 1980. The marriage was vehemently opposed by the racist South African government, which bullied Britain's Labour party into exiling the royal couple from Bechuanaland in 1951. The king's uncle and sometime regent, Tshekedi Khama, also tried and failed to have his nephew deposed. Williams, meanwhile, proved suprisingly popular in Africa.

## Summary

This article is centred on Wilf Mbanga and Trish Mbanga's Seretse and Ruth (2005), a Zimbabwean-authored, fictionalised biography of the first President of Botswana, Seretse Khama and his British wife, Ruth Williams. In the article, analysis of Seretse and Ruth is placed within the context of a resurgence of international interest both in Botswana as a society and in the marriage of the Khamas. The aims and methodology of Mbanga and Mbanga are compared to those of Michael Dutfield, the author of their main secondary source A Marriage of Inconvenience (1990). The ambiguity in the “play” on cultural and racial difference in Seretse and Ruth is discussed in an analysis of the biography's representation of Ruth and Seretse's courtship and the antagonism between Ruth and Seretse's uncle, Tshekedi.

Drawing on the work of Doris Sommer (1993) on the romance as foundational fiction in nineteenth-century Latin American writing, the paper argues that Seretse and Ruth presents the story of the Khamas as a foundational fiction in which “starcrossed lovers” from different races and regions eventually unite the new nation of Botswana. Moreover, the retelling of this story has resonances in contemporary southern African politics and culture. Seretse and Ruth contributes to the “myth” of Botswana as a successful, harmonious society that can be contrasted with the divided society of neighbouring Zimbabwe. The paper concludes that Seretse and Ruth presents a way of imagining a foundational fiction for Zimbabwe based on consensus rather than exclusion.
